items.mnemonic: Two crossbars and a loop: a mama holding a baby in her arms.
items.culture_note: ま comes from a cursive form of the kanji 末.

items.mnemonic: A musical note flowing to the right: 'mi', as in do-re-mi.
items.culture_note: み comes from a cursive form of the kanji 美.

items.mnemonic: A cow with a curly tail and a fly buzzing next to it: 'moo'.
items.culture_note: む comes from a cursive form of the kanji 武.

items.explanation: め is 'me', like the 'me' in 'met'. It looks like ぬ, but め has no loop at the end.
items.mnemonic: An eye with a line across it, and め on its own means 'eye' (目).
items.culture_note: め comes from a cursive form of the kanji 女.

items.explanation: も is 'mo', like 'mow' but pure. As a particle it means 'also' or 'too'.
items.mnemonic: A fishing hook with two bars across it, catching more and more fish.
items.culture_note: も comes from a cursive form of the kanji 毛. Momotarō, 'Peach Boy', is one of Japan's best-known folk tales: a boy born from a giant peach who sets out to defeat a band of ogres.
